evidence: ShoptOptions in crates/colony-expand/src/context.rs implements get(name: &str) -> Option<bool> and set(name: &str, value: bool) -> bool via exhaustive string-match dispatch (~25 fields each), duplicating what could be a typed struct with direct property access since the caller already knows the field name at call sites

The indirection hotspot scanner found 182 method-chain calls in colony-expand/src/context.rs with max_chain_depth 3, reflecting that ExpansionContext is accessed as a wide context bag by every expansion module (arithmetic, parameter, lib, pipeline, builtins, redirect, command_sub) through a uniform &mut ExpansionContext parameter

ProtocolEmitter in crates/colony-agent/src/agent.rs is a zero-field struct (Self {}) that wraps two trivial operations: emit_thought flushes stdout and emit_tool_call logs debug; it provides no protocol abstraction since the agent directly prints to stdout and the 'protocol' framing is unused

TreeProtocol in crates/colony-filetree/src/protocol.rs wraps a single TreeState field and exposes tree() / tree_mut() pass-through accessors alongside convert/emit methods; callers who need tree state could work with TreeState directly — the wrapper adds a thin translation layer but also leaks the inner via tree_mut()

McpConnectionPool.connection_state(), connected_servers(), server_names(), connected_count(), tool_count() in crates/colony-mcp/src/pool.rs each delegate directly to the inner connections HashMap with one-line bodies; these are read-only computed projections that add no policy — they are accessor forwarding

RecipeAgentConfig.merge_with_overrides() and apply_recipe_to_config() in crates/colony-agent/src/recipe_config.rs perform nearly identical field-by-field assignment from recipe fields to AgentConfig fields — two parallel paths that both flatten the same Recipe->AgentConfig translation, suggesting one could be eliminated

MemoryIntegration.is_enabled() in crates/colony-agent/src/memory_integration.rs returns self.config.enabled — a single-line getter that exposes a sub-field of a private config, adding a layer without added behavior

AgentTupleBridge.space() and .subscriptions() in crates/colony-agent/src/tuple_bridge.rs are pass-through accessors returning &self.space and &self.subscriptions respectively — callers receive the raw inner type and can use it directly, making the wrapper leaky

SidebarManager in crates/colony-ui-core/src/sidebar/manager.rs has several single-expression methods that route by SidebarPosition enum to left or right config fields (toggle, set_visible, is_visible, width) — these are justified by the two-sidebar design but the pattern repeats rather than generalizing

ProviderChain in crates/colony-agent/src/provider_chain.rs implements the ModelProvider trait by delegating all trait methods (supports_streaming, max_context_tokens, provider_name, model_name) to self.providers[active_index] — this is meaningful delegation since the chain adds fallback logic, but the non-complete trait methods do pure forwarding to active index without any chain reasoning

strengths: The feature-gated inner/stub pattern (recipe_config.rs, memory_integration.rs, tuple_bridge.rs) is a legitimate abstraction that isolates optional subsystems behind clean compile-time boundaries without leaking conditional logic into callers

ProviderChain correctly earns its abstraction — it implements the ModelProvider trait and adds meaningful fallback, health-tracking, and cooldown logic that callers genuinely benefit from rather than merely forwarding calls

RecipeLoader and RecipeRegistry are cohesive, focused types with no pass-through inflation: each method performs real work (filesystem traversal, manifest serialization, priority resolution) that would otherwise be scattered
The MCP connection pool (McpConnectionPool) adds genuine value: it routes tool calls to the right server, performs reconnection on failure, and aggregates tools across servers — not a thin wrapper

The expansion pipeline modules (arithmetic, parameter, lib) all accept &ExpansionContext directly and perform real work; the shared context is a necessary carrier for shell state, not gratuitous indirection
abstraction_fitness.issue_character: The codebase has a recurring pattern of thin accessor methods (is_enabled, space(), subscriptions(), connection_state() etc.) that expose inner-type fields or trivially delegate to sub-fields without adding policy, combined with a ShoptOptions string-dispatch get/set that mirrors what typed struct access already provides.
abstraction_fitness.score_rationale: The codebase scores above the midpoint because its major subsystem abstractions (ProviderChain, McpConnectionPool, RecipeLoader, feature-gated bridges) are genuine and pay for themselves. The score does not reach 80+ because there are several recurring thin-accessor and pass-through patterns — ProtocolEmitter as a zero-behavior wrapper, ShoptOptions string-keyed get/set duplicating struct field access, and multiple one-liner delegation methods that expose inner types — which add indirection without leverage. These are concentrated in a handful of files rather than systemic, keeping the score in the mid-70s rather than below 60.

issues.summary: ShoptOptions.get() and .set() implement string-keyed dispatch over struct fields that are already typeable by name
evidence: ShoptOptions::get(name: &str) -> Option<bool> contains a 25-arm match that maps string literals to struct field reads; the caller already knows the field by name at compile time in almost all call sites
ShoptOptions::set(name: &str, value: bool) -> bool is a parallel 25-arm match for writes; any typo or missing case is a silent None/false rather than a compile error

The only justification for string-keyed access is the shopt builtin which receives runtime strings from user input — that specific call site could receive the dispatch while all internal callers use direct field access
issues.suggestion: Keep the string dispatch methods only for the shopt builtin handler that receives runtime user strings. All internal callers that currently pass a string literal should access the struct fields directly (e.g., context.shopt.extglob instead of context.shopt.get("extglob")). This eliminates the runtime dispatch overhead and makes typos compile errors.

issues.summary: ProtocolEmitter is a zero-field struct whose two methods provide no protocol abstraction over raw stdout/debug
evidence: ProtocolEmitter is defined as `pub struct ProtocolEmitter {}` with no fields
emit_thought() calls print!() then flush() — the caller could do this directly
emit_tool_call() calls debug!() and returns Ok(()) — effectively a no-op wrapper over a logging call
The comment '// Emits OSC 2337 sequences for colony-terminal' suggests intended future behavior that was never implemented, leaving a placeholder abstraction in place
issues.suggestion: Either remove ProtocolEmitter and have Agent call stdout/tracing directly for the two call sites, or implement the OSC 2337 protocol it promises and make the abstraction earn its keep. As-is, it costs an indirection level for zero behavioral value.

issues.summary: RecipeAgentConfig.merge_with_overrides() and apply_recipe_to_config() both translate Recipe fields to AgentConfig fields with nearly identical logic
evidence: merge_with_overrides() builds an AgentConfig by first copying recipe values then overriding with user values — a two-pass field copy

apply_recipe_to_config() also copies recipe.prompt.system, recipe.model.temperature, and recipe.tools.approval.auto_approve into an existing AgentConfig — the same three fields, the same conditional logic
Both functions exist in the same module and handle the same translation domain; callers must decide which path to use without a clear protocol boundary
issues.suggestion: Consolidate to a single translation function. apply_recipe_to_config is the simpler form (in-place mutation); merge_with_overrides can call it internally, then apply overrides on top. This collapses two nearly-identical translation paths into one and makes the override semantics explicit rather than duplicated.

issues.summary: AgentTupleBridge.space() and .subscriptions() return references to inner types, making the wrapper leaky
evidence: space() -> &TupleSpace returns a plain reference to the inner TupleSpace; callers can call any TupleSpace method directly, bypassing the bridge's subscription notification logic
subscriptions() -> &SubscriptionManager similarly exposes the raw manager

write_tuple() and write_tool_result() both call self.space.out() AND self.subscriptions.notify() together — the bridge's value is that it keeps these two calls in sync; the accessors allow callers to call space.out() without notify(), breaking the invariant
issues.suggestion: Remove space() and subscriptions() from the public API or make them crate-private. Callers that need to read from the tuple space should use a dedicated read method on the bridge itself. If external callers genuinely need the full TupleSpace API, consider whether the bridge abstraction is appropriate at all.

issues.summary: MemoryIntegration.is_enabled() and .config() are single-field accessors over a private config struct
evidence: is_enabled() returns self.config.enabled — a one-liner that adds one indirection level for no policy
config() -> &MemoryConfig returns &self.config — a raw reference to the full config struct, exposing all config fields to callers anyway
If config() is public, callers can check config().enabled directly, making is_enabled() redundant
issues.suggestion: Remove is_enabled(); callers that already receive a &MemoryIntegration reference can call .config().enabled if needed, or check before constructing. Alternatively make the config field pub directly on MemoryIntegration since config() already exposes it.

root_causes: Several placeholder abstractions were created for future protocol work (ProtocolEmitter) that never materialized, leaving zero-behavior wrappers in production code
The ShoptOptions string-dispatch pattern was likely extracted from the bash builtin handler and generalized to all callers even when compile-time field access would be simpler and safer
Thin accessor methods (is_enabled, space, subscriptions) reflect a defensive encapsulation style where every private field gets a getter regardless of whether the getter adds behavior
possible_false_positives: SidebarManager.toggle/set_visible/is_visible position-routing methods — these repeat but the two-sidebar design makes them structurally necessary
ProviderChain delegation of supports_streaming/max_context_tokens to active provider — this is justified delegation within a fallback chain abstraction
